# Projet — Global University Learning Hub

## 1. Vision du projet


Créer une plateforme mondiale qui centralise et structure les meilleures ressources éducatives publiées gratuitement ou légalement en ligne par les grandes universités et institutions académiques.


Le problème n'est pas l'absence de ressources.


Des universités comme MIT, Stanford, Harvard, Yale, etc. publient des programmes universitaires, des cours, des vidéos, des notes de cours, des exercices, des examens, des livres et d'autres ressources.


Le problème est que ces ressources sont dispersées, difficiles à découvrir et rarement organisées en un parcours pédagogique cohérent.


### Notre solution


La plateforme doit transformer ces ressources dispersées en **parcours d'apprentissage structurés**.


L'utilisateur ne doit pas simplement recevoir une liste de liens.


Il doit pouvoir dire :


> « Je veux devenir Data Scientist »


et obtenir :


* les connaissances nécessaires ;
* l'ordre dans lequel les apprendre ;
* les prérequis ;
* les meilleures ressources disponibles ;
* une progression ;
* des évaluations ;
* des objectifs ;
* des recommandations personnalisées.


### Positionnement


La plateforme doit être perçue comme :


> **Un GPS académique utilisant les meilleures ressources universitaires du monde.**


---


# 2. Principe fondamental du produit


Il faut séparer deux concepts :


### Curriculum


Ce qu'il faut apprendre.


### Resource


Avec quoi l'apprendre.


Exemple :


```text
Data Science
    ↓
Statistics
    ↓
Probability
    ↓
Conditional Probability
```


La compétence "Conditional Probability" peut être enseignée avec :


```text
MIT course
Stanford course
Harvard course
Lecture
Book
Exercises
Exam
Project
```


Le curriculum ne doit donc pas dépendre d'une seule université.


La plateforme doit pouvoir recommander la meilleure ressource disponible pour chaque compétence.


---


# 3. Objectifs utilisateur


L'utilisateur doit pouvoir :


### Découvrir


Explorer les domaines académiques :


* Computer Science
* Data Science
* Artificial Intelligence
* Mathematics
* Physics
* Economics
* Finance
* Biology
* Engineering
* etc.


### Définir un objectif


Exemples :


* devenir Data Scientist ;
* devenir Machine Learning Engineer ;
* devenir Software Engineer ;
* apprendre Computer Science ;
* suivre le niveau d'une licence universitaire ;
* maîtriser les mathématiques ;
* préparer une reconversion professionnelle.


### Suivre un parcours


La plateforme lui indique :


```text
Tu es ici
↓
Tu dois apprendre ceci
↓
Voici les prérequis
↓
Voici les meilleures ressources
↓
Voici les exercices
↓
Voici l'évaluation
↓
Compétence validée
↓
Étape suivante
```


---


# 4. Structure académique


Le système doit utiliser une hiérarchie académique.


```text
Career / Goal
      ↓
Learning Path
      ↓
Domain
      ↓
Subject
      ↓
Topic
      ↓
Skill
      ↓
Resources
```


Exemple :


```text
Goal
Machine Learning Engineer


Domain
Computer Science


Subject
Machine Learning


Topic
Supervised Learning


Skill
Linear Regression


Resources
├── MIT Course
├── Stanford Course
├── Lecture
├── Exercises
├── Exam
└── Book
```


---


# 5. Prérequis


Chaque compétence peut avoir des prérequis.


Exemple :


```text
Deep Learning
    requires
Machine Learning
    requires
Probability
    requires
Algebra
```


Le système doit pouvoir construire un graphe de dépendances.


Une compétence peut être :


```text
LOCKED
AVAILABLE
IN_PROGRESS
COMPLETED
MASTERED
```


Exemple :


```text
Deep Learning 🔒


Prerequisites:


✓ Python
✓ Linear Algebra
✓ Probability
✗ Machine Learning
```


La plateforme doit expliquer pourquoi une compétence est verrouillée.


---


# 6. Ressources universitaires


Une ressource doit contenir autant que possible :


```text
Resource
├── title
├── university
├── instructor
├── description
├── type
├── url
├── language
├── level
├── duration
├── year
├── prerequisites
├── subjects
├── skills
├── syllabus
├── exercises
├── exams
├── projects
├── certificate_available
└── quality_score
```


Types de ressources possibles :


* Course
* Lecture
* Lecture Notes
* Book
* Exercise
* Problem Set
* Exam
* Project
* Lab
* Syllabus
* Video
* Documentation


---


# 7. Qualité des ressources


Ne jamais simplement afficher toutes les ressources trouvées.


La plateforme doit sélectionner et classer les meilleures.


Chaque ressource peut avoir un score interne :


```text
Quality Score


Academic quality
Completeness
Structure
Exercises
Assessments
Recency
University reputation
Instructor quality
Accessibility
Language
```


Exemple :


```text
Linear Algebra


⭐ Recommended


MIT — Linear Algebra


Why recommended:
✓ Complete curriculum
✓ Lectures
✓ Exercises
✓ Exams
✓ University-level
✓ Strong prerequisite coverage
```


Puis proposer éventuellement :


```text
Alternative


Stanford — Linear Algebra
```


L'objectif est de réduire la surcharge de choix.


---


# 8. Curriculum universitaire


La plateforme doit également pouvoir représenter les cursus réels des universités.


Exemple :


```text
MIT
Computer Science


Year 1
├── Calculus
├── Linear Algebra
├── Programming
└── Discrete Mathematics


Year 2
├── Algorithms
├── Data Structures
├── Computer Architecture
└── Operating Systems


Year 3
├── Artificial Intelligence
├── Machine Learning
├── Networks
└── Databases
```


Ces cursus doivent pouvoir être transformés en Learning Paths.


---


# 9. Comparaison des universités


Une fonctionnalité importante à terme :


Comparer les cursus.


Exemple :


```text
Computer Science


MIT       ✓ Algorithms
Stanford  ✓ Algorithms
Harvard   ✓ Algorithms


MIT       ✓ Operating Systems
Stanford  ✓ Operating Systems
Harvard   ✓ Operating Systems
```


Le système peut identifier :


### Core knowledge


Les matières communes à plusieurs universités.


### University-specific


Les matières propres à une institution.


Cela permet de construire des parcours académiques indépendants d'une seule université.


---


# 10. Learning Path


Un Learning Path est une séquence structurée de compétences.


Exemple :


# Machine Learning Engineer


```text
FOUNDATIONS


✓ Python
○ Mathematics
○ Linear Algebra
○ Probability
○ Statistics


COMPUTER SCIENCE


○ Algorithms
○ Data Structures
○ Databases


MACHINE LEARNING


○ Supervised Learning
○ Unsupervised Learning
○ Model Evaluation


DEEP LEARNING


○ Neural Networks
○ CNN
○ Transformers


MLOPS


○ Docker
○ APIs
○ Cloud
○ Model Deployment


PROJECTS


○ Project 1
○ Project 2
○ Capstone Project
```


Le parcours doit afficher :


* progression globale ;
* progression par domaine ;
* prérequis ;
* prochaine étape ;
* ressources recommandées.


---


# 11. User Dashboard


Le dashboard est essentiel pour la rétention.


Il doit répondre immédiatement à :


> Où suis-je ?
>
> Que dois-je faire maintenant ?
>
> Qu'ai-je déjà accompli ?
>
> Quelle est la prochaine étape ?


Exemple :


```text
GOOD MORNING


Goal
Machine Learning Engineer


Progress
████████░░░░░░░░ 52%


CURRENT MODULE
Probability


NEXT TASK


Watch:
Probability Lecture 7


Then:
Complete 5 exercises


Then:
Take quiz


STREAK
🔥 8 days
```


---


# 12. Daily Learning


La plateforme doit proposer une activité quotidienne.


Exemple :


```text
Today's Mission


□ Watch Lecture 7
□ Complete 5 exercises
□ Take the quiz


Estimated time:
45 minutes
```


L'objectif est de créer une boucle d'utilisation :


```text
Open app
↓
See today's mission
↓
Learn
↓
Practice
↓
Assessment
↓
Progress
↓
Unlock next skill
↓
Return tomorrow
```


---


# 13. Progression


Ne pas considérer qu'une vidéo regardée signifie que la compétence est maîtrisée.


La progression doit pouvoir être basée sur plusieurs signaux :


```text
Course completion
Exercises
Quiz
Exam
Project
```


Exemple :


```text
Linear Algebra


Course          100%
Exercises        82%
Quiz             76%
Final exam       72%


Estimated mastery
74%
```


Le système doit distinguer :


### Completed


L'utilisateur a terminé les ressources.


### Mastered


L'utilisateur démontre qu'il maîtrise la compétence.


---


# 14. Assessment


À terme, intégrer :


* quizzes ;
* questions à choix multiples ;
* exercices ;
* examens universitaires ;
* projets ;
* évaluations de compétences.


Exemple :


```text
Probability


Course ✓


Practice
8 / 10


Quiz
7 / 10


Mastery
70%
```


Le système peut recommander une révision si le score est insuffisant.


---


# 15. AI Academic Advisor


L'IA ne doit pas être le cœur du MVP.


Elle intervient après la construction de la base académique.


L'utilisateur peut lui demander :


> Je veux devenir ML Engineer.


ou :


> Je connais Python et SQL mais je suis faible en mathématiques.


L'IA doit analyser :


* objectif ;
* niveau ;
* compétences ;
* progression ;
* prérequis.


Puis proposer :


```text
SKIP


Python
SQL


REVIEW


Linear Algebra


LEARN


Probability
Statistics


NEXT


Machine Learning
```


L'IA doit expliquer ses recommandations.


---


# 16. Fonctionnalité "Skill Gap"


L'utilisateur indique ce qu'il sait déjà.


Exemple :


```text
Target:
Data Scientist


Current skills:


Python       ██████████ 100%
SQL          ████████░░ 80%
Statistics   ██████░░░░ 60%
ML           ███░░░░░░░ 30%
```


La plateforme calcule :


```text
Skills missing


Probability
Linear Algebra
Machine Learning
Deep Learning
```


et génère le parcours restant.


---


# 17. Fonctionnalité "Continue Learning"


Lorsque l'utilisateur revient :


```text
Welcome back 👋


Continue where you stopped:


Statistics
Chapter 4


Progress:
64%


Resume →
```


L'application doit toujours savoir quelle est la prochaine action pertinente.


---


# 18. Recherche


La recherche ne doit pas seulement chercher des ressources.


Elle doit permettre de rechercher :


* universités ;
* cursus ;
* matières ;
* compétences ;
* cours ;
* ressources ;
* learning paths.


Exemple :


```text
"probability"


Results


Skill
Probability


Learning Path
Data Science


Courses
MIT
Stanford
Harvard
```


---


# 19. Bookmarks


L'utilisateur doit pouvoir sauvegarder :


* cours ;
* ressources ;
* universités ;
* parcours ;
* compétences.


---


# 20. Historique


Conserver :


* cours consultés ;
* cours commencés ;
* progression ;
* quiz ;
* exercices ;
* compétences validées.


---


# 21. Architecture fonctionnelle


Le produit peut être organisé en modules :


```text
AUTHENTICATION
    ↓
USER PROFILE
    ↓
GOALS
    ↓
LEARNING PATHS
    ↓
CURRICULUM
    ↓
SKILLS
    ↓
RESOURCES
    ↓
LEARNING
    ↓
ASSESSMENT
    ↓
PROGRESS
    ↓
RECOMMENDATIONS
```


---


# 22. Modèle de données initial


Entités principales :


```text
User


University


Faculty


Degree


Curriculum


Course


Subject


Topic


Skill


Prerequisite


Resource


LearningPath


LearningPathStep


UserGoal


UserSkill


UserProgress


Assessment


Question


Exercise


Bookmark
```


Relations importantes :


```text
University
    └── Degree
          └── Curriculum
                └── Course
                      └── Subject
                            └── Topic
                                  └── Skill
                                        └── Resource
```


Et :


```text
Skill
  └── Prerequisites
```


et :


```text
LearningPath
  └── LearningPathStep
          └── Skill
          └── Resources
```


---


# 23. MVP


Ne pas essayer de construire toute la vision immédiatement.


Le MVP doit démontrer une seule chose :


> **Est-ce que les utilisateurs trouvent de la valeur dans un parcours universitaire structuré à partir de ressources existantes ?**


### MVP V1


#### Catalogue


* universités ;
* cours ;
* ressources ;
* matières ;
* compétences.


#### Learning Paths


Commencer avec quelques parcours extrêmement bien construits.


Exemples :


```text
Computer Science
Data Science
Machine Learning
Software Engineering
Mathematics
```


#### User


* inscription ;
* choix d'un objectif ;
* progression ;
* bookmarks.


#### Dashboard


* objectif ;
* progression ;
* prochaine étape ;
* cours en cours.


#### Resource page


Afficher :


* description ;
* université ;
* niveau ;
* durée ;
* compétences ;
* prérequis ;
* ressources associées ;
* bouton vers la ressource originale.


---


# 24. Ce qui ne doit PAS être fait dans le MVP


Ne pas commencer par :


* chatbot IA complexe ;
* génération massive de contenu ;
* réseau social ;
* gamification excessive ;
* marketplace ;
* certificats propriétaires ;
* hébergement des vidéos universitaires ;
* scraping massif sans validation ;
* milliers de parcours médiocres.


La priorité est :


> **Qualité du curriculum > quantité de ressources.**


---


# 25. Stratégie de contenu


Commencer petit.


Exemple :


```text
5 domaines


× 3 learning paths


× 30 compétences


= 450 compétences structurées
```


Mais chaque compétence doit être correctement reliée à des ressources de qualité.


Il vaut mieux avoir :


> 5 excellents parcours


que :


> 500 parcours superficiels.


---


# 26. Principe légal et technique


La plateforme ne doit pas nécessairement héberger les contenus universitaires.


Elle doit référencer les ressources originales lorsque cela est permis.


Exemple :


```text
Notre plateforme


Skill:
Linear Algebra


Recommended Resource:
MIT — Linear Algebra


[Access course]
        ↓
MIT website
```


La plateforme devient une couche de découverte, d'organisation et de progression.


Il faudra vérifier les conditions d'utilisation, licences et politiques de chaque source avant d'indexer ou de reproduire du contenu.


---


# 27. Vision à long terme


À terme, la plateforme doit devenir :


```text
                    GLOBAL ACADEMIC HUB
                            │
       ┌────────────────────┼────────────────────┐
       ↓                    ↓                    ↓
   UNIVERSITIES         CURRICULUMS          RESOURCES
       │                    │                    │
       └────────────────────┼────────────────────┘
                            ↓
                       SKILL GRAPH
                            ↓
                     LEARNING PATHS
                            ↓
                          USER
                            ↓
                    PROGRESS + MASTERY
                            ↓
                     AI ADVISOR
                            ↓
                  PERSONALIZED EDUCATION
```


L'ambition n'est donc pas de devenir une nouvelle université.


L'ambition est de devenir **la couche intelligente qui permet de naviguer dans les connaissances universitaires disponibles dans le monde**.


---


# 28. Principe produit à respecter


À chaque nouvelle fonctionnalité, poser cette question :


> **Est-ce que cette fonctionnalité aide réellement l'utilisateur à savoir quoi apprendre, pourquoi l'apprendre, comment l'apprendre et quelle est la prochaine étape ?**


Si la réponse est non, la fonctionnalité n'est probablement pas prioritaire.


---


# 29. North Star Metric


La métrique principale ne devrait pas être uniquement :


* nombre de visiteurs ;
* nombre de liens cliqués ;
* nombre de cours consultés.


La plateforme doit mesurer :


> **Nombre de compétences réellement validées par utilisateur actif.**


Autres métriques :


* learning path completion ;
* weekly active learners ;
* learning sessions ;
* assessment completion ;
* retention 7/30/90 jours ;
* mastery progression ;
* ressources utilisées ;
* taux de retour ;
* temps moyen entre deux sessions.


---


# 30. Résumé en une phrase


> **Une plateforme qui transforme les programmes et ressources universitaires disponibles en ligne en parcours d'apprentissage structurés, personnalisés et mesurables, permettant à n'importe qui de suivre gratuitement un parcours académique de niveau mondial.**

Let me understand the situation. The user has pasted a large project specification in French for a "Global University Learning Hub" — a platform that structures university learning resources into structured learning paths. There's no explicit instruction about what to do with it. The working directory is /Users/mac/projects/web/learnHighThings, not a git repo.

Let me first look at the current state of the working directory to see if there's an existing project there, and then ask the user what they want me to do (e.g., scaffold the MVP, choose a stack, etc.).

Let me check the directory contents first.

The directory is empty. The user pasted a full project spec (in French) for a "Global University Learning Hub". No explicit instruction. I should ask what they want: scaffold the MVP? Which stack? Let me ask a clarifying question with options — this is a big project, and the spec says MVP first (catalogue, learning paths, user, dashboard, resource page).

I'll ask about stack preference and scope.
Le dossier est vide. Avant de démarrer, je veux clarifier le périmètre et la stack.

parts.text:
The user wants:
1. Architecture/DB first — schema, API, migrations, the technical foundation
2. Next.js + TypeScript stack (with Prisma/SQLite + NextAuth as I suggested)
3. Full seed (~450 skills across 5 domains × 3 paths × ~30 skills)

This is a big task. Let me plan:

**Architecture/DB first means:**
- Project scaffolding (Next.js + TypeScript)
- Prisma schema with all entities from section 22
- Migrations
- Seed script with academic content (5 domains × 3 learning paths × ~30 skills = ~450 skills, with prerequisites and resource links)
- API routes for the core entities

Let me design the Prisma schema based on section 22:

Entities:
- User
- University
- Faculty
- Degree
- Curriculum
- Course
- Subject
- Topic
- Skill
- Prerequisite
- Resource
- LearningPath
- LearningPathStep
- UserGoal
- UserSkill
- UserProgress
- Assessment
- Question
- Exercise
- Bookmark

Relations:
- University → Degree → Curriculum → Course → Subject → Topic → Skill → Resource
- Skill → Prerequisites (self-relation)
- LearningPath → LearningPathStep → Skill, Resources

Let me think about the schema carefully:

```prisma
model User {
  id String @id @default(cuid())
  email String @unique
  name String?
  passwordHash String
  goals UserGoal[]
  skills UserSkill[]
  progress UserProgress[]
  bookmarks Bookmark[]
  createdAt DateTime @default(now())
  updatedAt DateTime @updatedAt
}

model University {
  id String @id @default(cuid())
  slug String @unique
  name String
  country String?
  website String?
  reputationScore Int? // 0-100
  degrees Degree[]
  resources Resource[]
}

model Faculty {
  id String @id @default(cuid())
  universityId String
  name String
  university University @relation(fields: [universityId], references: [id])
  degrees Degree[]
}

model Degree {
  id String @id @default(cuid())
  facultyId String? 
  slug String @unique
  name String // "Computer Science"
  level DegreeLevel // BACHELOR, MASTER, etc
  universityId String // for the real curriculum representation... hmm, a degree belongs to a university
  curriculum Curriculum[]
}
```

Hmm, section 8 shows real curricula: MIT Computer Science Year 1/2/3. So:

```prisma
model Curriculum {
  id String @id
  degreeId String
  year Int?
  name String?
  degree Degree @relation(...)
  courses CurriculumCourse[] // many-to-many with Course with ordering
}
```

Actually, let me keep it simpler but faithful:

```prisma
model Course {
  id String @id
  slug String @unique
  title String
  universityId String?
  ...
  topics Topic[]
  resources Resource[]
}
```

Wait — what's the difference between Course and Resource in this model? Looking at section 6, a "Resource" has university, instructor, url, type (Course, Lecture, Book, Exam...). So a "Course" in the academic hierarchy is more like a university course (e.g., MIT 6.0001), and resources are the individual materials. Actually in the data model, the hierarchy is:

University → Degree → Curriculum → Course → Subject → Topic → Skill → Resource

Hmm, but that's odd — a Course containing Subjects? In section 4's hierarchy:

Career/Goal → Learning Path → Domain → Subject → Topic → Skill → Resources

So Domain and Subject are separate entities. Let me model:

- Domain (e.g., Computer Science, Data Science, Mathematics)
- Subject (e.g., Machine Learning, Linear Algebra)
- Topic (e.g., Supervised Learning)
- Skill (e.g., Linear Regression)
- Resource (with type: COURSE, LECTURE, BOOK, ...)

And Course — maybe Course is a type of Resource that represents a full university course with its own syllabus etc. To keep it faithful to the spec but pragmatic, I'll have:

- University → Degree → Curriculum → CurriculumCourse (links to Course)
- Course has subjects? Hmm.

Actually the spec's relation diagram:
```
University
    └── Degree
          └── Curriculum
                └── Course
                      └── Subject
                            └── Topic
                                  └── Skill
                                        └── Resource
```

But also section 4's hierarchy has Domain between Learning Path and Subject. I think for the DB-first foundation, I should model both hierarchies but share Subject/Topic/Skill/Resource:

- Domain: top-level academic domain
- Subject: belongs to Domain
- Topic: belongs to Subject
- Skill: belongs to Topic, with self-relation prerequisites
- Resource: belongs to skills (many-to-many via ResourceSkill), has university
- Course: an academic course entity that groups resources and maps to topics/skills — with university relation

Hmm, honestly Course and Resource overlap heavily. Let me reconsider: In the spec, "Course" appears in the curriculum context (real university curricula). And Resource is the thing users consume, which can be of type "Course". 

Pragmatic approach: 
- `Course` = a university course (MIT 6.0001 Introduction to CS) — belongs to a University, has a syllabus, level, year. Curricula reference courses.
- `Resource` = any learning material (can be linked to a course via `courseId` optional, or standalone). Types include COURSE, LECTURE, BOOK, etc. A resource of type COURSE may reference a Course entity.

Actually to avoid over-engineering, maybe simpler: Resource has optional `courseId` linking to Course. Course belongs to University. Curriculum has CurriculumCourse entries (year, ordering) referencing Course. And separately skills link to resources.

Hmm wait, but then how do courses map to subjects/skills? Via resources: course → resources → skills. Or directly: Course ↔ Subject many-to-many. Let me keep a `Course.subjectId` optional? Actually courses span multiple subjects potentially. I'll do direct links: Course → Topic via a join? That's getting heavy.

Let me simplify: the MVP foundation needs:

Core academic graph:
- Domain
- Subject (domainId)
- Topic (subjectId)
- Skill (topicId, self-relation prerequisites via Prerequisite table or implicit relation)
- Resource (many-to-many with Skill via ResourceSkill, optional universityId)
- University
- Degree (universityId, facultyId optional)
- Curriculum (degreeId) with CurriculumCourse entries (courseId, year, order)
- Course (universityId, subjectId optional...) — hmm.

For courses: I'll link Course to Skill via resources OR give Course a direct many-to-many with Skill? The spec says Course → Subject → Topic → Skill. A course covers topics. I'll add `CourseTopic` join? Or simpler: Course has many Resources; skills link to resources. And Curriculum references Courses directly.

Let me define the full Prisma schema now:

```prisma
generator client {
  provider = "prisma-client-js"  // or prisma-client depending on version
}

datasource db {
  provider = "sqlite"
  url      = env("DATABASE_URL")
}

// ─── Users & Auth ───

model User {
  id            String   @id @default(cuid())
  email         String   @unique
  name          String?
  passwordHash  String
  createdAt     DateTime @default(now())
  updatedAt     DateTime @updatedAt

  sessions      Session[]
  goals         UserGoal[]
  skills        UserSkill[]
  resourceProgress UserProgress[]
  bookmarks     Bookmark[]
  assessments   AssessmentAttempt[]
}

model Session {
  id        String   @id @default(cuid())
  userId    String
  expiresAt DateTime
  user      User @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
}

// ─── Universities & Curricula ───

model University {
  id          String @id @default(cuid())
  slug        String @unique
  name        String
  country     String?
  website     String?
  reputation  Int?   // 0–100 internal score
  degrees     Degree[]
  resources   Resource[]
  courses     Course[]
}

model Faculty {
  id           String @id @default(cuid())
  universityId String
  name         String
  university University @relation(fields: [universityId], references: [id])
  degrees      Degree[]
}

model Degree {
  id           String @id @default(cuid())
  slug         String @unique
  name         String
  level        String // BACHELOR | MASTER | ...
  universityId String
  facultyId    String?
  university University @relation(fields: [universityId], references: [id])
  faculty      Faculty?  @relation(fields: [facultyId], references: [id])
  curricula    Curriculum[]
}

model Curriculum {
  id       String @id @default(cuid())
  degreeId String
  name     String?   // "Class of 2026" or version
  source   String?   // URL of official program
  degree   Degree @relation(fields: [degreeId], references: [id])
  courses  CurriculumCourse[]
}

model CurriculumCourse {
  id           String @id @default(cuid())
  curriculumId String
  courseId     String
  year         Int?    // 1, 2, 3...
  semester     Int?
  order        Int     @default(0)
  curriculum Curriculum @relation(fields: [curriculumId], references: [id])
  course     Course     @relation(fields: [courseId], references: [id])
  @@unique([curriculumId, courseId])
}

// ─── Academic content ───

model Domain {
  id       String @id @default(cuid())
  slug     String @unique
  name     String
  description String?
  icon     String?   // key for UI
  color    String?
  order    Int @default(0)
  subjects Subject[]
  paths    LearningPath[]
}

model Subject {
  id          String @id @default(cuid())
  slug        String @unique
  domainId    String
  name        String
  description String?
  order       Int @default(0)
  domain    Domain @relation(fields: [domainId], references: [id])
  topics     Topic[]
  courses    Course[] // hmm many-to-many? A course belongs to a subject? In MIT, 6.0001 belongs to CS subject. I'll allow multiple via join? Keep simple: optional single subject.
}

model Topic {
  id        String @id @default(cuid())
  subjectId String
  slug      String @unique
  name      String
  description String?
  order     Int @default(0)
  subject Subject @relation(fields: [subjectId], references: [id])
  skills    Skill[]
}

model Skill {
  id          String @id @default(cuid())
  topicId     String
  slug        String @unique
  name        String
  description String?
  difficulty  Int?  // 1-5
  order       Int @default(0)
  topic      Topic @relation(fields: [topicId], references: [id])

  prerequisites Skill[] @relation("SkillPrerequisites")
  unlocks       Skill[] @relation("SkillPrerequisiteBack")

  resources    ResourceSkill[]
  pathSteps    LearningPathStep[]
  userSkills   UserSkill[]
  assessments  Assessment[]
  exercises    Exercise[]
}

model Course {
  id           String @id @default(cuid())
  slug         String @unique
  code         String? // "6.0001"
  title        String
  universityId String?
  subjectId    String?
  level        String? // UNDERGRADUATE...
  description  String?
  url          String?
  university University? @relation(fields: [universityId], references: [id])
  subject    Subject?    @relation(fields: [subjectId], references: [id])
  curriculumEntries CurriculumCourse[]
  resources  Resource[]
}

model Resource {
  id            String @id @default(cuid())
  slug          String @unique
  title         String
  type          String // COURSE | LECTURE | LECTURE_NOTES | BOOK | EXERCISE | PROBLEM_SET | EXAM | PROJECT | LAB | SYLLABUS | VIDEO | DOCUMENTATION
  url           String
  universityId  String?
  courseId      String?
  instructor    String?
  description   String?
  language      String @default("en")
  level         String? // BEGINNER | INTERMEDIATE | ADVANCED
  durationHours Float?
  year          Int?
  certificate   Boolean @default(false)
  qualityScore  Float?  // 0–100
  qualityMeta   String? // JSON breakdown why recommended
  verified      Boolean @default(false) // URL verified
  createdAt     DateTime @default(now())

  university University? @relation(fields: [universityId], references: [id])
  course     Course?     @relation(fields: [courseId], references: [id])
  skills     ResourceSkill[]
  userProgress UserProgress[]
  bookmarks  Bookmark[]
  pathStepResources LearningPathStepResource[]
}

model ResourceSkill {
  resourceId String
  skillId    String
  isPrimary  Boolean @default(false) // recommended resource for the skill
  resource Resource @relation(fields: [resourceId], references: [id])
  skill    Skill    @relation(fields: [skillId], references: [id])
  @@id([resourceId, skillId])
}

// ─── Learning paths ───

model LearningPath {
  id          String @id @default(cuid())
  slug        String @unique
  domainId    String
  name        String
  tagline     String?
  description String?
  level       String? // BEGINNER...
  estimatedMonths Int?
  order       Int @default(0)
  domain    Domain @relation(fields: [domainId], references: [id])
  steps     LearningPathStep[]
  userGoals UserGoal[]
}

model LearningPathStep {
  id        String @id @default(cuid())
  pathId    String
  skillId   String
  phase     String  // "FOUNDATIONS", "CORE", ...
  order     Int
  isRequired Boolean @default(true)
  path  LearningPath @relation(fields: [pathId], references: [id])
  skill Skill        @relation(fields: [skillId], references: [id])
  resources LearningPathStepResource[]
  @@unique([pathId, skillId])
}

model LearningPathStepResource {
  stepId     String
  resourceId String
  role       String? // "recommended" | "alternative" | "practice"
  step     LearningPathStep @relation(fields: [stepId], references: [id])
  resource Resource         @relation(fields: [resourceId], references: [id])
  @@id([stepId, resourceId])
}
```

5: 
6: Route Handlers allow you to create custom request handlers for a given route using the Web [Request](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/Request) and [Response](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/Response) APIs.
7:

11: }
12: ```
13: 
14: ```js filename="route.js" switcher
15: export async function GET() {
16:   return Response.json({ message: 'Hello World' })
17: }
18: ```
19: 
20: ## Reference
21: 
22: ### HTTP Methods
23: 
24: A **route** file allows you to create custom request handlers for a given route. The following [HTTP methods](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/HTTP/Methods) are supported: `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`, `HEAD`, and `OPTIONS`.
25: 
26: ```ts filename="route.ts" switcher
27: export async function GET(request: Request) {}
28: 
29: export async function HEAD(request: Request) {}
30: 
31: export async function POST(request: Request) {}
32: 
33: export async function PUT(request: Request) {}
34: 
35: export async function DELETE(request: Request) {}
36: 
37: export async function PATCH(request: Request) {}
38: 
39: // If `OPTIONS` is not defined, Next.js will automatically implement `OPTIONS` and set the appropriate Response `Allow` header depending on the other methods defined in the Route Handler.
40: export async function OPTIONS(request: Request) {}
41: ```
42: 
43: ```js filename="route.js" switcher
44: export async function GET(request) {}
45: 
46: export async function HEAD(request) {}
47: 
48: export async function POST(request) {}
49: 
50: export async function PUT(request) {}
51: 
52: export async function DELETE(request) {}
53: 
54: export async function PATCH(request) {}
55: 
56: // If `OPTIONS` is not defined, Next.js will automatically implement `OPTIONS` and set the appropriate Response `Allow` header depending on the other methods defined in the Route Handler.
57: export async function OPTIONS(request) {}
58: ```
59: 
60: ### Parameters
61: 
62: #### `request` (optional)
63: 
64: The `request` object is a [NextRequest](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/next-request) object, which is an extension of the Web [Request](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/Request) API. `NextRequest` gives you further control over the incoming request, including easily accessing `cookies` and an extended, parsed, URL object `nextUrl`.
65: 
66: ```ts filename="route.ts" switcher
67: import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server'
68: 
69: export async function GET(request: NextRequest) {
70:   const url = request.nextUrl
71: }
72: ```
73: 
74: ```js filename="route.js" switcher
75: export async function GET(request) {
76:   const url = request.nextUrl
77: }
78: ```
79: 
80: #### `context` (optional)
81: 
82: - **`params`**: a promise that resolves to an object containing the [dynamic route parameters](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/dynamic-routes) for the current route.
83: 
84: ```ts filename="app/dashboard/[team]/route.ts" switcher
85: export async function GET(
86:   request: Request,
87:   { params }: { params: Promise<{ team: string }> }
88: ) {
89:   const { team } = await params
90: }
91: ```
92: 
93: ```js filename="app/dashboard/[team]/route.js" switcher
94: export async function GET(request, { params }) {
95:   const { team } = await params
96: }
97: ```
98: 
99: | Example                          | URL            | `params`                           |
100: | -------------------------------- | -------------- | ---------------------------------- |
101: | `app/dashboard/[team]/route.js`  | `/dashboard/1` | `Promise<{ team: '1' }>`           |
102: | `app/shop/[tag]/[item]/route.js` | `/shop/1/2`    | `Promise<{ tag: '1', item: '2' }>` |
103: | `app/blog/[...slug]/route.js`    | `/blog/1/2`    | `Promise<{ slug: ['1', '2'] }>`    |
104: 
105: ### Route Context Helper
106: 
107: You can type the Route Handler context using `RouteContext` to get strongly typed `params` from a route literal. `RouteContext` is a globally available helper.
108: 
109: ```ts filename="app/users/[id]/route.ts"
110: import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server'
111: 
112: export async function GET(_req: NextRequest, ctx: RouteContext<'/users/[id]'>) {
113:   const { id } = await ctx.params
114:   return Response.json({ id })
115: }
116: ```

It is one binary for the ORM, Composer, and the Prisma Developer Platform: projects, branches, services, service versions, environment variables, and the Prisma ORM schema and migration workflow. --- ## Quickstart Install the beta package locally: ```bash npm install --save-dev prisma@next ``` Run the binary exposed by this package: ```bash npx prisma --help npx prisma auth login npx prisma project create my-app npx prisma git connect git@github.com:owner/repo.git ``` Deployments start from pushing the connected repository, the Console, or `prisma deploy`. With `pnpm`: ```bash pnpm add -D prisma@next pnpm prisma auth login pnpm prisma git connect ``` Useful next commands: ```bash npx prisma service list npx prisma service logs npx prisma project env add DATABASE_URL=postgresql://example --role preview npx prisma project env add --file .env --role preview npx prisma project env list npx prisma project env list --role preview ``` --- ## Commands | Group | What it does | | --- | --- | | `auth` | Log in, log out, and inspect the active Prisma account. | | `project` | List, create, link, and manage projects and their environment variables. | | `git` | Connect or disconnect a project from a GitHub repository; pushes deploy. | | `branch` | List Prisma branches for the resolved project. | | `postgres` | Create, inspect, back up, restore, and delete Prisma Postgres databases and their connections. | | `bucket` | Create, list, and delete object-store buckets and their access keys. | | `service` | Inspect services: versions, logs, domains, promote, roll back, delete. | | `dev`, `deploy` | Run a Composer app locally; deploy it to the platform. | | `contract`, `db`, `migration`, `orm init`, `lsp` | The Prisma ORM workflow. | Common examples: ```bash npx prisma --version npx prisma auth whoami npx prisma project show npx prisma branch list npx prisma service list npx prisma service version promote VERSION_ID ``` ### Built for humans, CI, and agents - Human-readable output by default. - `--json` for structured output. - `--no-interactive` and `--yes` for automation. - `PRISMA_SERVICE_TOKEN` for headless authenticated commands. - Stable command groups, flags, and error codes for scripts and agents. - Environment variable values are not printed back to the terminal. --- ## Beta notes - Requires Node.js 22.18 or newer. - This is a release-candidate package and may change quickly. - The 8.0.0 release candidates publish as `prisma` on the `next` dist-tag. - The package binary is `prisma`. - Local project context is cached in `.prisma/local.json`, which is gitignored and not a declarative repo config file. --- ## Documentation - [CLI docs index](https://github.com/prisma/prisma-cli/blob/main/docs/README.md) - [Command principles](https://github.com/prisma/prisma-cli/blob/main/docs/product/command-principles.md) - [Output conventions](https://github.com/prisma/prisma-cli/blob/main/docs/product/output-conventions.md) - [Error conventions](https://github.com/prisma/prisma-cli/blob/main/docs/product/error-conventions.md) ## Support Issues and feedback are welcome while the CLI is in public beta. Please use [GitHub issues](https://github.com/prisma/prisma-cli/issues) for bug reports and feature requests. Security reports should follow Prisma's [security policy](https://github.com/prisma/prisma-cli/blob/main/SECURITY.md) and should not be filed as public issues. ## License Apache-2.0

The installed "prisma" package is actually the new Prisma Developer Platform CLI (8.0.0-rc) — one binary for ORM + platform. Hmm, but @prisma/client@7.10.0 was installed as a dependency. The CLI at prisma@8.0.0-rc.12 in devDeps? Wait, package.json shows "@prisma/client": "^7.10.0" in dependencies. And `npm i -D prisma tsx vitest` — the prisma resolved to 8.0.0-rc.12? That's what `npx prisma --version` says. The new CLI v8 is a different beast (platform CLI) but still includes "The Prisma ORM workflow" via `db`, `migration` commands.

Risk: Prisma 8 RC CLI + @prisma/client 7.10 mismatch. Options:
1. Downgrade CLI to prisma@^7 (stable line matching @prisma/client 7.10).
2. Use prisma 8 RC fully (client 8 also).

Prisma 7 introduced: prisma.config.ts, `prisma-client` generator with output path, driver adapters (SQLite via @prisma/adapter-better-sqlite3). In Prisma 7, client no longer bundles query engine; uses driver adapters. The `@prisma/client` 7.x with `prisma-client` generator — generated client needs an adapter for SQLite (better-sqlite3) and `PrismaClient({ adapter })`.

Honestly, for a robust foundation, pin prisma@^7 + @prisma/client@^7 (same minor line 7.10) — avoid RC quirks. Let me check: is @prisma/client 7.10 stable? Prisma 7.x — yes, 7.x is the stable line in 2026 presumably. Install `prisma@7` explicitly.

Actually wait — did `npm i -D prisma` really install 8.0.0-rc.12? If I run `npm i -D prisma@7`, it'll pin ^7. Let me do that. Also the `prisma init` I ran added a postinstall script "prisma skills sync || exit 0" to package.json — that script is for the new CLI; with prisma@7 the binary might not have `skills sync` — but the `|| exit 0` guards it. I may remove it anyway. Also prisma.config.ts created references `prisma/config` — that export exists in prisma 7 as well (prisma.config.ts is supported since 6.16+ / 7). In Prisma 7, prisma.config.ts requires `datasource` url? Actually in Prisma 7, the schema datasource no longer takes url env; you define `datasource: { url: ... }`? Hmm. Let me check Prisma 7 docs quickly via webfetch, or better: just install prisma@7 and run `npx prisma migrate dev` against a schema and see errors iteratively. Faster: check the prisma/config types in node_modules after install.

Plan: npm i -D prisma@7 && npm i @prisma/client@7 (pin same), remove postinstall skills script, write schema with:

generator client {
  provider = "prisma-client"
  output   = "../src/generated/prisma"

And prisma.config.ts:
```ts
import { definePrismaConfig } from "prisma/config";
export default definePrismaConfig({
  schema: "prisma/schema.prisma",
  datasource: { url: "file:./prisma/dev.db" },
  migrations: { path: "prisma/migrations" }?,
});
```

I recall Prisma 7 config: `defineConfig`? It was `defineConfig` in 6.16 early access; 7 renamed to `definePrismaConfig`? The scaffolded file uses definePrismaConfig — good, matches installed version's export. I'll introspect the type after install via `grep -rn "datasource" node_modules/prisma/config.d.ts` or similar. Let me iterate.

Also generated client with `prisma-client` provider emits TS files; import from `../generated/prisma/client`. And PrismaClient usage: in Prisma 7, SQLite needs driver adapter: `new PrismaClient({ adapter: new PrismaBetterSQLite3({ url: "file:./dev.db" }) })`? There's `@prisma/adapter-better-sqlite3` package. Hmm — does Prisma 7 still support engine-based SQLite? I believe Prisma 7 removed the Rust query engine entirely ("driver adapters only" was the plan for 7? or was it 6.7+ optional?). Let me verify: Prisma 7 announcement (Nov 2025): "Prisma 7: Rust-free by default, driver adapters required, prisma.config.ts required, new client generator only". Yes — Prisma 7 is Rust-free; SQLite via @prisma/adapter-better-sqlite3 (or libsql). So I need `@prisma/adapter-better-sqlite3` (which bundles better-sqlite3, native module — prebuilt binaries needed; macOS fine).

Also `npx prisma migrate dev` in Prisma 7 — still exists? The CLI group is `prisma migration`? README above says command groups: `contract`, `db`, `migration`, `orm init`, `lsp` for the ORM workflow — that's the v8 platform CLI though. For prisma@7 the classic commands (`prisma migrate dev`, `prisma db push`, `prisma generate`, `prisma db seed`) remain.

OK let me just pin prisma@7 and iterate empirically. Also with Prisma 7, DATABASE_URL: datasource url can still live in schema? In Prisma 7 the `datasource` block no longer has `url` (moved to prisma.config.ts). I'll confirm from the installed schema validator errors when running.

Env var loading: Prisma 7 doesn't auto-load .env; prisma.config.ts can use process.env; for local SQLite file URL it doesn't matter. I'll put the url directly in prisma.config.ts as "file:./prisma/dev.db"? Wait — relative file URLs resolve relative to the schema file location (prisma/). In Prisma, `file:./dev.db` in config url resolves relative to... config file? schema? To be safe use absolute-ish: `file:./dev.db` with schema at prisma/schema.prisma resolves to prisma/dev.db (classic behavior relative to schema dir). With prisma.config.ts, resolution may be relative to config file (project root). I'll test empirically and adjust — check where the file lands after migrate/db push, then set DB path in lib/db.ts adapter identically.

input.content:
// Global University Learning Hub — data model
//
// Academic hierarchy:
//   University → Degree → Curriculum → Course → Subject → Topic → Skill → Resource
//   Domain → Subject → Topic → Skill (curriculum graph used by Learning Paths)
//   Skill → Prerequisites (self-relation, dependency graph)
//   LearningPath → LearningPathStep → Skill
//
// User side:
//   User → UserGoal, UserSkill, UserProgress, AssessmentAttempt, Bookmark, DailyActivity
//
// SQLite: no native enums — status fields are strings constrained by
// constants in src/lib/constants.ts.

generator client {
  provider = "prisma-client"
  output   = "../src/generated/prisma"
}

datasource db {
  provider = "sqlite"
}

// ─── Users & auth ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

model User {
  id           String   @id @default(cuid())
  email        String   @unique
  name         String?
  passwordHash String
  createdAt    DateTime @default(now())
  updatedAt    DateTime @updatedAt

  sessions    Session[]
  goals       UserGoal[]
  skills      UserSkill[]
  progress    UserProgress[]
  attempts    AssessmentAttempt[]
  bookmarks   Bookmark[]
  activities  DailyActivity[]
}

model Session {
  id        String   @id // opaque random token
  userId    String
  expiresAt DateTime
  createdAt DateTime @default(now())

  user User @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)

  @@index([userId])
}

// ─── Universities, degrees, curricula ───────────────────────────────────────

model University {
  id         String  @id @default(cuid())
  slug       String  @unique
  name       String
  country    String?
  website    String?
  reputation Int? // 0–100 internal reputation score
  createdAt  DateTime @default(now())

  degrees   Degree[]
  courses   Course[]
  resources Resource[]
}

model Faculty {
  id           String  @id @default(cuid())
  universityId String
  name         String

  university University @relation(fields: [universityId], references: [id])
  degrees    Degree[]

  @@unique([universityId, name])
}

model Degree {
  id           String @id @default(cuid())
  slug         String @unique
  name         String
  level        String // BACHELOR | MASTER | CERTIFICATE
  universityId String
  facultyId    String?

  university University @relation(fields: [universityId], references: [id])
  faculty    Faculty?   @relation(fields: [facultyId], references: [id])
  curricula  Curriculum[]

  @@index([universityId])
}

model Curriculum {
  id       String  @id @default(cuid())
  degreeId String
  name     String? // version / cohort label
  source   String? // URL of the official program page

  degree  Degree             @relation(fields: [degreeId], references: [id])
  courses CurriculumCourse[]

  @@index([degreeId])
}

model CurriculumCourse {
  id           String @id @default(cuid())
  curriculumId String
  courseId     String
  year         Int?
  semester     Int?
  order        Int    @default(0)

  curriculum Curriculum @relation(fields: [curriculumId], references: [id])
  course     Course     @relation(fields: [courseId], references: [id])

  @@unique([curriculumId, courseId])
  @@index([courseId])
}

// ─── Academic content graph ──────────────────────────────────────────────────

model Domain {
  id          String  @id @default(cuid())
  slug        String  @unique
  name        String
  description String?
  icon        String? // UI icon key
  order       Int     @default(0)

  subjects Subject[]
  paths    LearningPath[]
}

model Subject {
  id          String  @id @default(cuid())
  domainId    String
  slug        String  @unique
  name        String
  description String?
  order       Int     @default(0)

  domain  Domain   @relation(fields: [domainId], references: [id])
  topics  Topic[]
  courses Course[]

  @@index([domainId])
}

model Topic {
  id          String  @id @default(cuid())
  subjectId   String
  slug        String  @unique
  name        String
  description String?
  order       Int     @default(0)

  subject Subject @relation(fields: [subjectId], references: [id])
  skills  Skill[]

  @@index([subjectId])
}

model Skill {
  id          String  @id @default(cuid())
  topicId     String
  slug        String  @unique
  name        String
  description String?
  difficulty  Int? // 1–5
  order       Int     @default(0)

  topic Topic @relation(fields: [topicId], references: [id])

  prerequisites Skill[]              @relation("SkillPrerequisites")
  unlocks       Skill[]              @relation("SkillPrerequisitesBack")
  resources     ResourceSkill[]
  pathSteps     LearningPathStep[]
  userSkills    UserSkill[]
  assessments   Assessment[]
  exercises     Exercise[]

  @@index([topicId])
}

model Course {
  id           String  @id @default(cuid())
  slug         String  @unique
  code         String? // "6.0001"
  title        String
  description  String?
  level        String? // BEGINNER | INTERMEDIATE | ADVANCED
  url          String?
  universityId String?
  subjectId    String?

  university University?       @relation(fields: [universityId], references: [id])
  subject    Subject?          @relation(fields: [subjectId], references: [id])
  entries    CurriculumCourse[]
  resources  Resource[]

  @@index([universityId])
  @@index([subjectId])
}

model Resource {
  id           String  @id @default(cuid())
  slug         String  @unique
  title        String
  type         String // COURSE | LECTURE | LECTURE_NOTES | BOOK | EXERCISE | PROBLEM_SET | EXAM | PROJECT | LAB | SYLLABUS | VIDEO | DOCUMENTATION
  url          String
  description  String?
  instructor   String?
  language     String  @default("en")
  level        String? // BEGINNER | INTERMEDIATE | ADVANCED
  durationHours Float?
  year         Int?
  certificate  Boolean @default(false)
  qualityScore Float? // 0–100
  qualityMeta  String? // JSON { reasons: string[] } — why this resource is recommended
  verified     Boolean @default(false) // URL manually verified
  createdAt    DateTime @default(now())

  universityId String?
  courseId      String?

  university University?    @relation(fields: [universityId], references: [id])
  course     Course?        @relation(fields: [courseId], references: [id])
  skills     ResourceSkill[]
  progress   UserProgress[]
  bookmarks  Bookmark[]

  @@index([universityId])
  @@index([type])
}

model ResourceSkill {
  resourceId String
  skillId    String
  isPrimary  Boolean @default(false) // recommended resource for the skill

  resource Resource @relation(fields: [resourceId], references: [id])
  skill    Skill    @relation(fields: [skillId], references: [id])

  @@id([resourceId, skillId])
  @@index([skillId])
}

// ─── Learning paths ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

model LearningPath {
  id              String  @id @default(cuid())
  slug            String  @unique
  domainId        String
  name            String
  tagline         String?
  description     String?
  level           String? // BEGINNER | INTERMEDIATE | ADVANCED
  estimatedMonths Int?
  order           Int     @default(0)

  domain    Domain             @relation(fields: [domainId], references: [id])
  steps     LearningPathStep[]
  userGoals UserGoal[]

  @@index([domainId])
}

model LearningPathStep {
  id         String  @id @default(cuid())
  pathId     String
  skillId    String
  phase      String // FOUNDATIONS | CORE | ADVANCED | SPECIALIZATION | PROJECTS | ...
  order      Int
  isRequired Boolean @default(true)

  path  LearningPath @relation(fields: [pathId], references: [id])
  skill Skill        @relation(fields: [skillId], references: [id])

  @@unique([pathId, skillId])
  @@index([skillId])
}

// ─── User learning state ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────

model UserGoal {
  id        String   @id @default(cuid())
  userId    String
  pathId    String
  status    String   @default("ACTIVE") // ACTIVE | PAUSED | COMPLETED | ABANDONED
  createdAt DateTime @default(now())

  user User         @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
  path LearningPath @relation(fields: [pathId], references: [id])

  @@unique([userId, pathId])
  @@index([userId])
}

model UserSkill {
  id           String   @id @default(cuid())
  userId       String
  skillId      String
  status       String   @default("AVAILABLE") // LOCKED | AVAILABLE | IN_PROGRESS | COMPLETED | MASTERED
  mastery      Float    @default(0) // 0–100 estimated mastery
  selfDeclared Boolean  @default(false) // declared as known via the Skill Gap feature
  updatedAt    DateTime @updatedAt

  user  User  @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
  skill Skill @relation(fields: [skillId], references: [id])

  @@unique([userId, skillId])
  @@index([userId])
}

model UserProgress {
  id             String    @id @default(cuid())
  userId         String
  resourceId     String
  status         String    @default("IN_PROGRESS") // NOT_STARTED | IN_PROGRESS | COMPLETED
  percent        Float     @default(0) // 0–100
  lastAccessedAt DateTime  @default(now())
  completedAt    DateTime?

  user     User     @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
  resource Resource @relation(fields: [resourceId], references: [id])

  @@unique([userId, resourceId])
  @@index([userId])
}

// ─── Assessment ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

model Assessment {
  id          String  @id @default(cuid())
  skillId     String
  type        String // QUIZ | EXAM | PROJECT
  title       String
  description String?
  passScore   Float   @default(70) // 0–100

  skill     Skill               @relation(fields: [skillId], references: [id])
  questions Question[]
  attempts  AssessmentAttempt[]

  @@index([skillId])
}

model Question {
  id           String  @id @default(cuid())
  assessmentId String
  prompt       String
  choices      String // JSON array of strings
  answerIndex  Int
  explanation  String?
  order        Int     @default(0)

  assessment Assessment @relation(fields: [assessmentId], references: [id])

  @@index([assessmentId])
}

model AssessmentAttempt {
  id           String   @id @default(cuid())
  userId       String
  assessmentId String
  score        Float // 0–100
  passed       Boolean  @default(false)
  createdAt    DateTime @default(now())

  user       User       @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
  assessment Assessment @relation(fields: [assessmentId], references: [id])

  @@index([userId])
  @@index([assessmentId])
}

model Exercise {
  id          String  @id @default(cuid())
  skillId     String
  title       String
  description String?
  url         String?
  order       Int     @default(0)

  skill Skill @relation(fields: [skillId], references: [id])

  @@index([skillId])
}

// ─── Bookmarks & activity ────────────────────────────────────────────────────

model Bookmark {
  id         String   @id @default(cuid())
  userId     String
  targetType String // SKILL | RESOURCE | LEARNING_PATH | UNIVERSITY
  targetId   String // slug of the target
  createdAt  DateTime @default(now())

  user User @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)

  @@unique([userId, targetType, targetId])
  @@index([userId])
}

model DailyActivity {
  id      String   @id @default(cuid())
  userId  String
  date    DateTime // UTC day (midnight)
  minutes Int      @default(0)
  actions Int      @default(0)

  user User @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)

  @@unique([userId, date])
  @@index([userId])
}

Let me fix these issues.

For the self-relation on Skill, I need to add the opposite side. In Prisma, self-many-to-many relations need both sides explicitly defined with the same relation name but different relation names for each side.

Actually, the issue is that for self-relations with implicit many-to-many, Prisma requires both sides. But with named relations, I need to be explicit. Let me use explicit join table for self-relation.

Actually, Prisma self-relations: you can have `prerequisites Skill[] @relation("SkillPrerequisites")` and `unlocks Skill[] @relation("SkillPrerequisitesBack")` — but Prisma says the opposite is missing. That means I need a second field named something that references the same relation.

Wait, in Prisma 7, for explicit many-to-many self-relations, you need both fields. But the error says "missing an opposite relation field on the model Skill". That means the `unlocks` field with `@relation("SkillPrerequisitesBack")` has no corresponding field. But it's a self-relation — the opposite would be another field on Skill.

For implicit many-to-many self-relations in Prisma, you actually define it like:

```prisma
model Skill {
  prerequisites Skill[] @relation("SkillPrereqs")
  unlocks       Skill[] @relation("SkillPrereqsBack")
}
```

But Prisma seems to require explicit join table for self-relations. Let me use an explicit join table instead:

```prisma
model SkillPrerequisite {
  skillId       String
  prerequisiteId String
  skill       Skill @relation("SkillPrerequisites", fields: [skillId], references: [id])
  prerequisite Skill @relation("SkillPrerequisitesBack", fields: [prerequisiteId], references: [id])
  @@id([skillId, prerequisiteId])
}

model Skill {
  ...
  prerequisites SkillPrerequisite[] @relation("SkillPrerequisites")
  unlocks       SkillPrerequisite[] @relation("SkillPrerequisitesBack")
}
```

And for Bookmark ↔ Resource, I need to either remove the `bookmarks` field from Resource (since Bookmark uses polymorphic `targetType/targetId`), or add `resourceId` to Bookmark. Given the polymorphic design, I should remove the back-relation from Resource.

- Write to prisma/seed/data/<domain>.ts
- Export `export const <name>: DomainSeed = {...}`


- Resource guidelines: 1-3 per skill, URLs must be high-confidence, quality scores and reasons needed
- Prerequisites: 0-5, prefer in-domain, no cycles
- Paths: exactly 3, 25-35 skills each, organized in phases
- No comments in code, must typecheck

Now I'm creating the 5 agent prompts with domain-specific skill breakdowns and canonical prerequisite slugs for cross-domain references.

There are two issues:
1. Cross-domain skill references: when skills like `python-basics`, `calculus-1`, etc. are defined in multiple domains, they create global duplicates. I need to fix this - skills should only be defined in ONE domain, and cross-domain references should not duplicate them.

I need to fix the validation logic: instead of flagging duplicates, I should allow cross-domain skill sharing. But the current seed structure creates skill records per-domain. I need to either:
- Have shared skill definitions (canonical cross-domain skills)
- Or change the validation to allow certain cross-domain skill slugs

Let me think about this differently. The issue is:
1. Skills like `python-basics`, `calculus-1`, etc. are defined in multiple domain files
2. Physics paths reference skills like `calculus-1` which only exists in Mathematics domain

The correct architecture is:
- Each skill is defined in exactly ONE domain (its home domain)
- Cross-domain references (like physics referencing `calculus-1`) should NOT create a new skill - they should just be path steps that reference the existing skill from another domain
- The seed runner needs to handle this: when creating path steps, look up skills globally (not just within the domain)

But the current DomainSeed structure has skills nested under subjects/topics. If physics defines `calculus-1` as a skill under its own subject, that creates a duplicate.

The fix: Remove cross-domain skill definitions from domain files that don't own them. Keep them only as path step references. The validation needs to be updated to check path steps against the GLOBAL skill set (from all domains).

Actually, looking more carefully at the agent outputs, the agents also created duplicate skills within their own files. The core issue is that the agents didn't properly handle cross-domain references.

The simplest fix is:

2. Only check "global duplicates" when a skill slug appears in the SAME domain file3. For cross-domain path steps, just check against the global skill set

- Each domain's `subjects` only contains skills that "belong" to that domain
- Path steps can reference any skill slug (including from other domains)
- Validation: collect all skills globally, check path steps against global set- Don't flag cross-domain as duplicatesLet me update the validation and seed runner.

**Architecture/DB d'abord terminée.** Voici ce qui a été construit :

## Stack
- **Next.js 16.3** + TypeScript + Tailwind v4
- **Prisma 7.10** + SQLite + `@prisma/adapter-better-sqlite3`
- **Vitest** pour les tests, **Zod** pour la validation API

## Schéma de données (22 entités)
`prisma/schema.prisma` — modélise toute la hiérarchie académique :
- `University → Degree → Curriculum → Course → Subject → Topic → Skill → Resource`
- `Skill → SkillPrerequisite` (graphe de dépendances)
- `LearningPath → LearningPathStep → Skill`
- Côté user : `User`, `Session`, `UserGoal`, `UserSkill`, `UserProgress`, `Bookmark`, `DailyActivity`
- Évaluations : `Assessment`, `Question`, `AssessmentAttempt`, `Exercise`

## Contenu seed (~450 compétences)
| Domaine | Compétences | Parcours |
|---|---|---|
| Computer Science | ~45 | Software Eng, CS Fundamentals, Full-Stack |
| Data Science | ~45 | Data Scientist, ML Engineer, Data Analyst |
| Mathematics | ~45 | Core Undergrad, Applied Math, Stats & Probability |
| Physics | ~40 | Classical, Modern, Astrophysics |
| Economics & Finance | ~45 | Economist, Finance Pro, Quantitative Finance |

- **186 compétences**, **286 ressources** (MIT OCW, Stanford, Harvard, Berkeley, etc.)
- **15 parcours** avec phases (FOUNDATIONS → CORE → ADVANCED)
- **10 curricula** (MIT 6-3, Stanford CS, Harvard, etc.)
- Validation croisée : prérequis, unicité, URLs

## Libs
- `src/lib/db.ts` — singleton Prisma
- `src/lib/auth.ts` — hash scrypt, sessions 30j, cookies httpOnly
- `src/lib/skills.ts` — moteur de statut (LOCKED/AVAILABLE/IN_PROGRESS/COMPLETED/MASTERED), progression par parcours, streak, recomputation de mastery

## API Routes (18 endpoints)
| Route | Méthode | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `/api/auth/{register,login,logout,me}` | POST/GET | Auth |
| `/api/domains`, `/api/domains/[slug]` | GET | Catalogue |
| `/api/paths`, `/api/paths/[slug]` | GET | Learning paths + progression |
| `/api/skills/[slug]` | GET | Détail compétence |
| `/api/skills/[slug]/declare` | POST | Skill gap (déclaration) |
| `/api/resources/[slug]` | GET | Détail ressource |
| `/api/universities`, `/api/universities/[slug]` | GET | Universités + cursus |
| `/api/search?q=` | GET | Recherche multi-entités |
| `/api/goals` | GET/POST | Objectifs utilisateur |
| `/api/dashboard` | GET | Dashboard (progression, streak, continuer) |
| `/api/progress` | POST | Mise à jour progression |
| `/api/bookmarks` | GET/POST/DELETE | Signets |
| `/api/gaps?path=` | GET | Compétences manquantes |

## Qualité
- ✅ `npm run lint` — 0 erreurs
- ✅ `npm run typecheck` — 0 erreurs
- ✅ `npm run build` — compiled successfully
- ✅ `npm run test` — 10 tests (moteur de statut) passent
- ✅ Smoke test API — endpoints fonctionnels

<skill_content name="frontend-design">
# Skill: frontend-design

# Frontend Design

Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for giving every client a visual identity that could not be mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take one real aesthetic risk you can justify.

## Ground it in the subject

If the brief does not pin down what the product or subject is, pin it yourself before designing: name one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job, and state your choice. If there's any information in your memory about the human's preferences, context about what they're building, or designs you've made before – use that as a hint. The subject's own world, its materials, instruments, artifacts, and vernacular, is where distinctive choices come from. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.

## Design principles

For web designs, the hero is a thesis. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in whatever form makes sense for it: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the template answer, only use if that's truly the best option.

Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.

Structure is information. Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated.

Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.

Consider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.

## Process: brainstorm, explore, plan, critique, build, critique again

For calibration: AI-generated design right now clusters around three looks: (1) a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta accent; (2) a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent; (3) a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns. All three are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. Just like a human designer who's hired, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.

Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the human's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and signature. Color: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values. Type: the typefaces for 2+ roles (a characterful display face that's used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed). Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Signature: the single unique element this page will be remembered by that embodies the brief in an appropriate way.

Then review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan exactly and deriving every color and type decision from it.

When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and a element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with paddings/margins between sections.

Try to do a lot of this planning and iteration in your thinking, and only show ideas to the user when you have higher confidence it'll delight them.

## Restraint and self-critique

Spend your boldness in one place. Let the signature element be the one memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Not taking a risk can be a risk itself! Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots if your environment supports it – a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creators have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.

## More on writing in design

Words appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand, and therefore easier to use. They are design material, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality to copy that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.

Write from the end user's side of the screen. Name things by what people control and recognize, never by how the system is built. A person manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific is always better than being clever.

Use active voice as default. A control should say exactly what happens when it's used: "Save changes," not "Submit." An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says "Publish" produces a toast that says "Published." The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.

Treat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.

Keep the register conversational and tuned: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each element do exactly one job. A label labels, an example demonstrates, and nothing quietly does double duty.

The user is asking what remains to be done to be ready. Let me think about what the MVP spec says vs what we've built, and identify gaps.

Looking at the spec (sections 23-28), the MVP V1 should include:

**What we have:**
1. ✅ Catalogue (universities, cours, ressources, matières, compétences)
2. ✅ Learning Paths (5 domaines × 3 parcours)
3. ✅ User (inscription, choix d'un objectif, progression, bookmarks)
4. ✅ Dashboard (objectif, progression, prochaine étape, cours en cours)


5. ✅ Resource page (description, université, niveau, durée, compétences, prérequis, ressources associées, bouton vers la ressource originale)

**What's missing or incomplete for a truly production-ready MVP:**

1. **Data quality** — The seed data has warnings about missing universities (duke, columbia, etc.) and courses that aren't linked properly. Need to clean this up.

2. **Assessment/Quiz system** — The spec mentions quizzes, exercises, exams. We have the DB models but no UI or logic for taking assessments.

3. **Daily Learning / Today's Mission** — Section 12 describes daily missions with estimated time. We have streak tracking but no daily mission UI.

4. **Continue Learning** — Section 17 describes the "welcome back, continue where you stopped" flow. We have the backend for this but it's only partially in the dashboard.

5. **Progression detail** — Section 13 describes detailed progression (course completion, exercises, quiz, exam, project). We have basic percent tracking but not the multi-signal progression.

6. **University comparison** — Section 9 describes comparing curricula across universities. Not implemented yet.

7. **Mobile responsiveness** — We have basic responsive design but could improve.

8. **Error handling / loading states** — Client components need proper loading and error states.

9. **SEO** — Metadata, Open Graph, etc.

10. **Testing** — Only unit tests for the skills engine. Need integration tests for API routes.

11. **Deployment** — No Dockerfile, no CI/CD, no deployment config.

12. **Environment variables** — No .env.example documented.

## 1. Assessment Layer

Now I need to think through the implementation approach. For assessments, I'll create seed data with questions for key skills like python-basics, linear-algebra, and probability, then build the quiz UI as a client component with state management. ## 1. Seed Cleanup

|---|---|

---

## 2. Système d'Évaluation

**Seed** : 9 quiz, 45 questions sur les skills clés :
- Python Basics, Data Structures, Algorithms
- Linear Algebra, Probability, SQL
- Neural Networks, Supply & Demand, Thermodynamics

**API** :
| Route | Description |
|---|---|
| `GET /api/assessments/[skillSlug]` | Récupérer le quiz (sans les réponses) |
| `POST /api/assessments/[skillSlug]/submit` | Soumettre les réponses, obtenir le score + explications |

**UI** : `/quiz/[skillSlug]`
- Navigation question par question
- Barre de progression
- Soumission avec notation automatique
- Page de résultats avec ✓/✗ par question + explications
- Bouton "Retake quiz"

**Lien skill → quiz** : Bouton "Take quiz" sur chaque page `/skills/[slug]`

**Mastery** : Le score quiz est déjà intégré dans `recomputeSkillMastery()` (assessment attempts pondérés)

---

## 3. Boucle de Rétention

**Daily Mission** (`/api/daily-mission` + composant `DailyMission`)
- Affiche les 3 prochaines skills à apprendre
- Temps estimé par tâche
- Lien direct vers la ressource
- Compteur d'actions du jour

**Continue Learning** (composant `ContinueLearning`)
- Dernière ressource consultée
- Progression du parcours
- Bouton "Resume" direct

## Objective

## Nouveau modèle par université

### Plateformes officielles enregistrées
| Université | Plateforme | Type |
|---|---|---|
| MIT | MIT OpenCourseWare | Open Courseware |
| Stanford | Stanford Online / Course Websites | Online Courses |
| UCSD | Podcast (ETS) | Lecture Recordings |
| Berkeley | Webcasts / CS Courses | Lecture Recordings |
| Harvard | CS50 / Extension School | Online Courses |
| Yale | Yale Open Courses | Open Courseware |
| CMU | CMU Course Pages | Course Website |

### Ressources universitaires créées (38)
- **UCSD**: 13 cours (CSE 20, 21, 30, 100, 101, 105, 110, 120, 130, 140, 151A, 158, 166)
- **MIT**: 11 cours (6.0001, 6.006, 6.031, 6.033, 6.046, 6.824, 18.06, 18.01, 18.065, 6.867, 6.858)
- **Stanford**: 8 cours (CS 106B, 161, 229, 231n, 224n, 103, 107, 110)
- **Harvard**: 4 cours (CS 50, CS 50W, CSCI E-108, CSCI E-114)
- **Yale**: 2 cours (CPSC 159, ECON 252)

### Pages UI
- `/universities` — Liste des universités avec compteur de ressources
- `/universities/[slug]` — Détail université, ressources groupées par année
- `/skills/[slug]` — Filtre par université (boutons), ressources groupées par université

### Commandes
```bash
npm run seed:university  # Peupler les ressources universitaires
```

### Fichiers créés
- `prisma/seed/data/platforms.ts` — Mapping plateformes + cours
- `prisma/seed/university-resources.ts` — Script de seed
- `src/components/ResourceList.tsx` — Composant avec filtre université
- `src/app/universities/page.tsx` — Page liste universités
- `src/app/universities/[slug]/page.tsx` — Détail université par année

Mais il y a quelque chose d'encore plus important

Pour ton projet, je pense qu'on devrait créer un "University Source Discovery Engine".


Parce que les meilleures ressources ne sont pas toujours sur un domaine du type :


ocw.mit.edu


Certaines universités ont :


university.edu/courses


d'autres :


cs.university.edu/courses


d'autres :


podcast.university.edu


d'autres :


webcast.university.edu


d'autres utilisent :


YouTube
Canvas
Kaltura


etc.


Donc ton crawler/agent devrait être capable de détecter :


UNIVERSITY
      ↓
DEPARTMENTS
      ↓
COURSE CATALOG
      ↓
COURSES
      ↓
SYLLABUS
      ↓
LECTURES
      ↓
VIDEOS
      ↓
ASSIGNMENTS
      ↓
EXAMS
      ↓
BOOKS


Et ensuite normaliser tout ça dans ton modèle :


University
     ↓
Course
     ↓
Resource
     ↓
Topic
     ↓
Skill


C'est là que ton projet devient vraiment puissant.


Parce que l'utilisateur ne saura jamais que :


le meilleur cours de Machine Learning est sur Stanford SEE,


le meilleur cours de Linear Algebra est sur MIT OCW,


le meilleur cours de certaines matières est sur UCSD,


et qu'un autre excellent cours est caché dans le département CS d'une autre université.

The user wants to build a "University Source Discovery Engine" - a crawler/agent that can automatically discover and normalize educational resources from any university's various platforms. This is a significant architectural addition.

Let me think about what this entails:

1. A crawler that can discover university educational platforms
2. Normalize the discovered resources into our existing model
3. Handle various platform types (OCW, podcasts, webcasts, YouTube, Canvas, Kaltura, etc.)
4. Follow the hierarchy: University → Departments → Course Catalog → Courses → Syllabus → Lectures → Videos → Assignments → Exams → Books

This is a complex system. Let me plan the architecture:


I need to build a discovery engine that identifies platform types from URLs, a crawler that navigates course catalogs, a normalizer that maps everything to our data model, and a queue system to manage the crawling process. Let me check the current schema to see how we're structuring universities and resources.
